# Notes on the 1979 gearbox

The gearbox arrived in a milk crate. No paperwork, no photos, just a note from Dennis that said "runs, sort of" — which I have since learned is Dennis's way of saying it does not run.

I spent Saturday taking it apart on the kitchen table, which my wife tolerated for exactly as long as it took the first bearing to hit the floor and roll under the fridge. Second gear was the problem. You could feel it: a catch, then nothing, then a lurch as the dogs finally bit. Third and fourth were fine. First was fine. Second felt like chewing gravel.

Here is the thing nobody tells you about these boxes — the synchro rings are not the wear item. Everyone assumes they are. They're brass, they look sacrificial, and every forum post from 2004 tells you to replace them and move on. I replaced mine. It changed nothing.

The actual culprit was the selector fork. Bent maybe two millimetres, which is not enough to see and is absolutely enough to feel. Somebody had driven it hard, probably for years, and the fork had slowly taken a set. Once I laid a straightedge across it the whole thing was obvious.

I measured it against the new one:

```
old fork:  47.2mm at the pad, 2.1mm deflection
new fork:  47.2mm at the pad, 0.0mm deflection
```

Two millimetres. Eleven hours of my life.

Reassembly took another weekend, mostly because I dropped a circlip into the bellhousing and refused, on principle, to buy another one. I found it Sunday afternoon. It was inside the crate the whole time.

Does it work? Yes. Second gear engages like it should — a clean, positive click, no gravel. Dennis was right, in his way. It did run. Sort of.

The lesson, if there is one, is that the cheap obvious part is rarely the broken part. It's just the one you can reach.
